title: Reading notes: LLM inference papers + conference takeaways
content:
Quick summary / purpose:
These are my notes from reading recent papers, blog posts, and conference talks relevant to reducing latency/cost for Redwood inference runtime. Focus areas: KV/cache strategies, speculative decoding, quantization tradeoffs, and batching/autoscaling heuristics. Mostly informal - TODOs at the bottom.

1) KV cache sharding & eviction (paper + blog synth)
- Problem: very large KV caches blow GPU memory when we keep long session histories across many concurrent users.
- Approaches summarized:
  - Sharded KV across multiple GPUs with on-demand prefetching (keep only working set local). Good for long contexts but increases inter-GPU comms.
  - TTL-based eviction: TTL per-session / per-prefix, heuristics based on last-access time + prefix popularity. Simple and robust in real traffic.
  - LRU / frequency + size-aware eviction: tradeoff between accuracy and compute cost to maintain stats.
  - Compressed KV (FP16/INT8) for cold regions: reduce memory but need decode overhead.
- Takeaway for Redwood: prefer a hybrid: LRU-ish in local GPU caches for low latency, with optional async prefetch to keep long-tail sessions off-GPU in compressed form. Provide per-customer policy (retain X tokens or TTL).
- Experiment idea: simulate session access traces from hosted API logs for a week and measure miss-rate vs memory usage for different TTLs/shard sizes.

2) Speculative decoding (paper + implementation notes)
- Basic idea: run a cheap model (e.g., 1-2B) to propose next tokens and validate them with the large model; reduces rounds of autoregressive decoding and total large-model steps.
- Observed gains: 20-40% latency reduction on some workloads (depends on proposal quality and validation batch efficiency).
- Integration notes for Redwood:
  - Need a multi-model route: fast model colocated on same node or separate pool with very low-comm path.
  - Validation step can be batched across many requests to amortize cost. This fits Redwood's batching runtime if we can align validation windows.
  - Failure modes: when proposal quality is low (domain shift), speculative decoding can add overhead. Need dynamic gating: only use spec-decoding for routes with baseline acceptance > threshold.
- TODO: prototype with distil/gpt2-like proposer + gpt-variant verifier using our local benchmark prompts. Track end-to-end latency + token cost.

3) FlashAttention / sparse-kernel optimizations / memory-friendly attention
- Papers and open-source kernels show 2-5x speedups for attention with reduced memory footprint (FlashAttention-style streaming).
- For Redwood serving runtime: benefits mostly for medium to long sequences where attention memory dominates. Kernel choice should be dynamic: small seq -> default fast path; long seq -> flash path.
- Caveat: GPU kernel availability varies by hardware and driver; need fallback and per-node capability detection.

4) Quantization: PTQ vs QAT, per-channel scales, and calibration sets
- Post-training quant (INT8/qat-lite) works well for many decoder-only LLMs for inference (especially with activation calibration). But performance varies by ops and layer types.
- Per-channel quantization for weights generally better than per-tensor for large layers. Activation quantization needs representative calibration traces (prompt shapes matter!).
- Practical note: shipping quantized model variants as fallback in Redwood Dedicated/Private is attractive - huge cost savings, but need automatic quality/regression checks (sample prompts + eval set).
- Action: add a small quant-eval pipeline (100-1000 eval prompts per customer route) and integrate with Optimize recommendations.

5) Batching, autoscaling, and latency SLOs (conference talk notes)
- Observation: optimized batching must be workload-aware (prompt length distribution + tail-latency SLO). Blindly maximizing tokens/sec increases tail latency.
- Autoscaler should be sensitivity-aware: ramp up quickly on latency tail or queue depth, but drain slower to avoid oscillation.
- Practical heuristics from talk: use percentiles (p95/p99) of queued-request waiting time as primary trigger, not just GPU utilization. Also add cooldown windows tuned per-customer SLA.

Misc links I keep returning to:
- arXiv/flashattention, spec-decoding blog posts, and a couple of open-source quant toolkits (QLoRA-ish notes).
- Internal: GH issue for speculative decoding prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/issues/456

Open questions / unknowns:
- How does spec-decoding interact with our multi-tenant batching? Will verification batching hurt the fast path?
- Can we realistically maintain compressed cold KVs on host memory + async prefetch without increasing 95th latency?
- Where to surface quantized-model regressions to product teams (Console + Optimize)?

Immediate TODOs (short):
- [ ] Simulate KV cache eviction policies with 1-week production trace (assign to me).
- [ ] Prototype speculative-decoding POC (small proposer + verifier) and run on 1000 prompt sample set. (pair w/ Lena)
- [ ] Add 200-sample quant-eval harness to Optimize pipeline; metric: semantic-similarity drop + token-cost delta.
- [ ] Draft short doc for eng sync on runtime kernel-selection logic (when to pick FlashAttention path).

Longer-term / backlog:
- integrate speculative decoding into route config (per-route enable + uphill model selection), with safe fallback to standard decode.
- implement per-customer KV retention policies + telemetry (cache hit rate dashboards).

Notes to self: stick to small experiments, measure end-to-end cost and p99 latency, not just op-level speedups. Discuss with SRE about prefetch traffic patterns (Slack #serving-runtime).

References / quick bib (save links locally):
- "FlashAttention" (arXiv) - kernel approaches for memory-efficient attention.
- "Speculative Decoding" blog/paper - faster autoregressive generation via verifier model.
- QLoRA / post-training quant blogs and repos.

End.

Contact / follow-ups: ping Lena or Samira if you want to collaborate on any of the above. I will sync this into the eng meeting notes if we have traction by next week.
